abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Cis-acting regulatory enhancer elements are powerful tools for achieving cell type-specific genetic access in adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery platforms. However, a significant bottleneck in enhancer discovery remains the accurate characterization of their in vivo expression patterns, which currently relies on labor-intensive, gold-standard one-by-one validation. Here, we evaluate multiple barcoded, multiplexed strategies for accelerated profiling of enhancer-driven expression at cell type resolution. As a proof-of-concept, we test small pools of well-validated enhancer AAVs with known activity across diverse cell types in the mouse brain. Despite extensive optimization and testing, we encounter substantial technical and biological noise, including chimeric AAV packaging products, that obscure true enhancer expression patterns. These effects are particularly pronounced for weaker enhancers and enhancers active in less abundant cell subpopulations. These findings highlight the challenges inherent to multiplexed enhancer AAV screening, the importance of careful enhancer pool design, and the complexity of enhancer AAV biology in vivo.

sec.p: Subject terms: Genetic vectors, Expression systems, Gene expression profiling, High-throughput screening

abstract.p: Massively parallel reporter assays promise rapid in vivo characterization of enhancer AAVs. Here, through systematic testing, authors uncover pervasive technical and biological noise, including chimeric AAV species, that exposes fundamental limitations in pooled enhancer screening.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Enhancers are cis-acting DNA elements that interact with transcription factors to increase the probability of endogenous gene expression. Depending on the chromatin state and transcription factors present, enhancer-driven gene expression in vivo can be highly cell-type- and region-dependent. Recent advancements in single-cell sequencing technologies have facilitated large-scale enhancer identification across cell classes, subclasses, and types through the integration of cell type classification with epigenomic discovery1,2. Machine learning algorithms trained on large genomic datasets can accurately predict enhancer activity based on sequence motifs, chromatin accessibility, and epigenetic modifications3,4. Importantly, these putative enhancer sequences are portable into synthetic contexts and can be packaged with a minimal promoter into enhancer AAVs capable of driving cell type-specific gene expression5. These efforts have resulted in a large toolbox containing thousands of enhancer AAVs for targeting diverse cell types across the brain6–12.

To validate enhancer AAVs as functional tools in the brain, the most prominent and reliable method is laborious one-by-one testing. This involves pairing novel enhancer sequences with fluorescent reporters, individual AAV packaging and in vivo injections, and examining each enhancer independently for on-target cell type specificity and expression patterns. This screening approach requires an enormous amount of time, effort, and animals, making it challenging to perform duplicates or troubleshoot when enhancer AAVs exhibit unpredicted expression patterns. Parallelizing or multiplexing enhancer AAVs for validation would not only accelerate the screening process but may also provide avenues for retesting or optimizing enhancers with unexpected expression.

Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) enable simultaneous evaluation of thousands of putative enhancer sequences by detecting enhancer-driven mRNA transcripts, either through enhancer-paired short DNA sequences (“barcodes”) or by using the enhancer sequence itself as a unique identifier8,13–16. These barcoded or enhancer sequence polyadenylated transcripts can be effectively captured in RNA sequencing assays, allowing enhancer expression patterns to be assessed in vivo within a single animal.

To establish multiplex enhancer screening in-house, we assemble a pool of well-validated, cell type-specific enhancers. Each enhancer is paired with small mRNA barcodes (mBCs) in the 3’ untranslated region (UTR), packaged into AAVs, injected as a pool into mice, and assayed using droplet-based RNA sequencing to detect enhancer-driven expression. In contrast to previous screens that focused primarily on unknown regulatory elements or capsids8,17–20, we observe unexpectedly poor enhancer specificities, leading to a systematic investigation of potential confounders that mask true enhancer expression.

Through our search, we identify and describe the impact of several major sources of noise, including weak detection of AAV-derived transcripts, packaging chimeras (see also Lalanne et al., co-submitted21), and transcriptional crosstalk between enhancer AAVs22. Although we implement multiple strategies to reduce background noise and improve mBC detection, our multiplex screen still fails to fully recapitulate the performance observed with individual enhancer testing, particularly for enhancers active in restricted cell subpopulations. Together, these results highlight the intrinsic challenges of multiplex enhancer screening and underscore the need for continued methodological optimization to achieve accurate and reliable characterization of enhancer AAVs.

sec.title: Design of a multiplex enhancer AAV validation pipeline in the mouse brain
sec.p: Enhancer AAV validation is a multi-step process involving cloning enhancer elements into reporter vectors, AAV packaging, in vivo delivery, and expression analysis (Fig. 1a, b). To establish a scalable workflow for robust enhancer-driven transcript recovery and accurate cell type identification, we implemented a multiplexed testing strategy in which each mouse is injected with a pool of enhancer AAVs.

sec.p: To test our multiplex strategy, we selected eighteen previously validated and published Allen Institute enhancers with high specificity for their intended cell type targets (greater than 70% on-target specificity)2,6,7,12 (Fig. 1c–g). This diverse pool included five glial enhancers, with two astrocyte (AiE0387m and AiE0390m) and three oligodendrocyte (AiE0391h, AiE0401h, and AiE0410m) enhancers, and thirteen neuronal enhancers. Seven of the neuronal enhancers had regional expression patterns, with six labeling different cell populations in the striatum (pan-MSN enhancers AiE0450h, and AiE0447h; D2 MSN enhancers AiE0452h and AiE0445h_3xC2; D1 MSN enhancer AiE0779m; striatal cholinergic enhancer AiE0743m_3xC2) and one labeling parvalbumin (Pvalb) chandelier cells, a subpopulation of Pvalb interneurons in the cortex (AiE0475m). Three enhancers express broadly in neuronal classes, including two forebrain GABAergic enhancers (hI56i and the optimized version, DLX2.0), and one pan-excitatory enhancer (AiE0078h). The last three enhancers labeled interneurons in multiple brain regions, including inhibitory Pvalb interneurons (AiE0140h) and Sst Chodl interneurons (AiE0682h and AiE0600m).

Each enhancer was paired with a unique 8-base pair mRNA barcode (mBC), subcloned into a nuclear reporter vector (SYFP2-H2B), and packaged individually into PHP.eB, an AAV capsid variant known to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) in C57BL/6J mice23 (Fig. 1h–k). We used immunohistochemistry and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (SMART-Seq v4, SSv4, see “Methods”) to confirm enhancers driving the new nuclear mBC construct closely matched the specificities of the originally published constructs also packaged in PHP.eB containing cytosolic SYFP2 (Fig. 1l, Supplementary Figs. 1–2 and Supplementary Data 1–3). All enhancers maintained high specificity for their intended cell type target, with a small trend towards lowered specificity with nuclear mBC constructs (Welch two sample t-test: P = 0.096; mean ± standard deviation: 86 ± 13% (mBC nuclear constructs) compared to 92 ± 10% (original constructs), Fig. 1m), possibly due to better detection of weakly (often off-target) expressing cells resulting from the higher signal-to-background ratio of the nuclear reporter compared to the cytosolic reporter (insets of Fig. 1e–g, i–k).

sec.title: Nuclear brain tissue preps are insufficient at capturing enhancer-driven AAV mBC transcripts in 10× Genomics RNA sequencing
sec.p: We next sought to establish a tissue dissociation method that would permit unbiased cell type recovery. Both whole cell and nuclear isolations are used widely in RNA sequencing24, although nuclei are often preferred due to simpler homogenization procedures and compatibility with frozen tissues.

We cloned the pan-neuronal promoter hSyn1 into the SYFP2-H2B-mBC screening vector and confirmed uniform SYFP2 expression throughout the brain following retro-orbital (RO) injection in mice (Fig. 2a–d). We generated whole cell and nuclear suspensions from the dorsal striatum (STR) and antero-lateral motor cortex (ALM), two brain regions enriched for long projection neurons that may exhibit differential recovery across prep methods24–26. Both SYFP2-positive and SYFP2-negative cells and nuclei were FACS-sorted and processed for single-cell or single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) using the 10× Genomics 3’ gene expression v3.1 platform. Cell types were assigned by mapping transcriptomes to a published whole mouse brain taxonomy27.

sec.p: We immediately observed pronounced differences in AAV mBC transcript recovery between whole cells and nuclei across both brain regions (Fig. 2e, f). While >90% of SYFP2-positive whole cells contained detectable AAV transcripts (mean ~12 UMIs per cell), fewer than 10% of SYFP2-positive nuclei showed any detectable transcripts (mean ~1 UMI per cell), despite high-quality nuclear libraries (Supplementary Fig. 3). To improve AAV transcript recovery, we generated an AAV-specific amplicon library by performing a semi-nested PCR on the 10x cDNA (AAV mBC library, Fig. 2g). This approach reliably recovered AAV transcripts from SYFP2-positive whole cell cDNA but required more amplification for nuclear cDNA and resulted in nonspecific detection of mBC transcripts in both SYFP2-positive and SYFP2-negative nuclear cDNA, consistent with off-target amplification of hSyn1-driven mBC transcripts in nuclei.

Given the concerns that whole cell preparations may preferentially lose fragile cell types, we compared recovered cell type proportions from scRNA-seq and snRNA-seq to neuronal populations in the published Allen Institute MERFISH mouse brain spatial atlas28 (Fig. 2h, i). Subclass proportions were largely comparable across modalities, with modest enrichment of PAL-STR_Gaba-Chol in snRNA-seq (Bonferroni-adjusted studentized t-test for regression, P < 0.05). Overall, subclass abundances were highly correlated (Pearson’s r: nuclei vs cells r = 0.884, cells vs. atlas r = 0.955), indicating minimal bias in neuronal cell type recovery.

We next tested multiple strategies to enhance nuclear retention of mBC AAV transcripts (Supplementary Fig. 4). These included vector modifications such as removal of the WPRE3 element, which has been reported to increase transcript stability and promote nuclear export29. Surprisingly, removal of WPRE3 negatively impacted transcript recovery in nuclei, significantly reducing AAV detection both at the protein and mRNA level (Supplementary Fig. 4a–g). We also evaluated whether minimizing freeze-thaw cycles during sample preparation would improve nuclear transcript recovery (Supplementary Fig. 4h–l), but observed no difference in mBC AAV transcript detection. Finally, we tested several nuclear retention motifs, including incorporation of the U7 scaffold system30,31, BORG lncRNA motif32, or SIRLOIN element33 (Supplementary Fig. 4m–r). These experiments were performed using the SSv4 snRNA-seq method that does not rely on GEM capture of polyA transcripts. However, none of these elements improved AAV transcript detection beyond ~50% of SYFP2+ nuclei. Without the ability to reliably detect the mBCs from nuclei, we only used whole cell preparations in all subsequent experiments.

sec.title: Individual AAV packaging is required for multiplexed screening in the brain
sec.p: We next designed a small multiplex using four of our highly specific enhancer AAVs for driving nuclear SYFP2 in distinct cell populations2,6,7 and two control promoters (hSyn1 and CMV) (Fig. 3a). All four enhancer AAVs included had greater than 95% on-target specificity when injected individually (specificities measured in Fig. 1l).

sec.p: We paired all six enhancers/promoters with unique mBCs and performed two separate AAV packaging procedures, the first resulting in six individual preps each with a single enhancer mBC vector, and the second a single pooled prep with all six enhancer mBC plasmids, similar to previous MPRAs14. Presence of all six mBCs was confirmed by deep sequencing the pooled plasmids, mixed individual AAV preps, and the single pooled AAV prep (see “Methods” and Supplementary Data 4). We injected the pooled prep and mixed individual preps intravenously by RO injection into mice separately and performed 10× Genomics scRNA-seq on whole cells isolated from the ALM and STR (Fig. 3b). We recovered the major neuronal and non-neuronal cell subclasses expected based on the enhancer pool (Fig. 3c) with similar cell type coverage and mBC detection between pooled and mixed individual prep libraries (Fig. 3d).

Analysis of AAV mBCs from the 10× cDNA (gene expression, GEX library) revealed poor detection of AAV transcripts, with most cells not containing any AAV mBCs at all. We thus generated an AAV-specific amplicon library (mBC library) that we confirmed to have robust UMI diversity (Supplementary Fig. 5) and increased mBC detection over the GEX library (~30% average increase in cells across both pooled and individual preps) (Supplementary Fig. 6a–c). Using presence of mBC alone (after performing sequence error correction using a threshold for Hamming distance ≤1) as an indication of enhancer expression, initial analysis suggested on-target enhancer specificities across both the GEX and mBC libraries were much lower than expected (mean <50% on-target cells compared to >95% by individual injection) for both the pooled and individual AAV preps.

We suspected that the low specificity arose from technical artifacts such as PCR chimeras, sequencing artifacts, or ambient RNA, supported by the bimodal distribution of enhancer mBC reads per UMI (Supplementary Fig. 6d–g) that others have also previously observed34. We therefore evaluated a range of read- and UMI-based filtering thresholds, and restricted analyses to cells with a single detected mBC. Despite these efforts, mean enhancer specificity did not exceed ~50% under any condition (Supplementary Fig. 6h).

To assess whether enhancer mBC UMIs correlated with SYFP2 protein expression, we compared enhancer mBC UMI counts with enhancer-driven SYFP2 expression levels obtained from the SSv4 flow sorts. However, we only observed a modest correlation between protein and UMIs that did not reach statistical significance (Pearson’s r, Individual Preps: r = 0.532, P = 0.28; Pooled Preps: r = 0.500, P = 0.31, Supplementary Fig. 6i). In contrast, UMI detection was highly correlated (Pearson’s r = 0.954, P = 0.0032) across AAV prep methods (Supplementary Fig. 6j). These results suggest that UMI detection may not accurately reflect enhancer-driven expression.

Although both packaging methods showed inaccuracies in enhancer specificity, several observations suggested additional fidelity issues associated with pooled packaging. First, the highly striatum-specific enhancer AiE0779m, which should serve as a functional negative control in ALM libraries, had significantly higher mBC UMI expression in ALM compared to STR in the pooled packaging libraries (Supplementary Fig. 6k). Second, across all filtering parameters, enhancers from pooled preps consistently exhibited a modest decrease in average specificity compared to individual preps (average 33% vs. 38% on-target specificity, respectively). Lastly, pooled packaged libraries exhibited significantly elevated mBC UMI levels in off-target cells compared to individual preps, despite comparable on-target UMI levels (Fig. 3e). These patterns indicate increased background noise in pooled AAV libraries.

We hypothesized that this additional source of noise arose during AAV packaging as all other experimental conditions were comparable between methods. To investigate this possibility, we performed long read sequencing directly on the AAV preps35 (Plasmidsaurus) (Fig. 3f). We found a substantial percentage (~37%) of reads from pooled AAV preps contained discordant enhancer-mBC pairings compared to only 2% in mixed individual preps (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Data 5). Similar levels of chimerism were observed across all three replicate packagings of the pooled six-plex library, consistent with independent findings (Lalanne et al., co-submitted21). These results indicate extensive enhancer-mBC recombination occurs during pooled AAV packaging and represents a major source of noise that compromises enhancer cell type specificity measurements in mBC-based enhancer AAV screens.

sec.title: A dual-barcoding error correction strategy to minimize technical noise
sec.p: Recently, our colleagues introduced single-cell quantitative expression reporters, (“scQers”, Fig. 4a), a dual-barcoding strategy designed to reduce technical noise through data-driven error correction36. This strategy incorporates a constitutively expressed small circular RNA “tornado barcode” (oBC) in addition to the enhancer-driven mBC (Fig. 4b). Concordant mBC-oBC pairs enable exclusion of unpaired mBCs, which are likely technical artifacts, thereby potentially improving specificity in multiplexed enhancer screens.

sec.p: We evaluated the scQer strategy in a twenty-plex enhancer AAV screen using two library designs. The first, termed “Single scQers” consisted of eighteen individually packaged enhancer AAVs plus two positive control promoter AAVs (twenty total, Fig. 4c–e), each containing a single unique oBC-enhancer-mBC. The second, termed “Multi scQers” was a moderately complex library of 3614 mBC-enhancer-oBC pairs, containing the same set of 20 enhancer AAVs but combined with approximately ~181 ± 52 (mean ± standard deviation) mBC-oBC pairs per enhancer (Fig. 4c). While the increased barcode diversity in the Multi scQer library could, in principle, enhance error-correction power, pooled packaging of this complex library resulted in AAV chimerism (see Lalanne et al., co-submitted21), increasing noise.

We delivered Single scQers or Multi scQers to mice by RO injection and performed scRNA-seq on sorted SYFP2-expressing whole cells from ALM and STR, as described above, alongside targeted sequencing of mBC and oBC amplicon libraries (Fig. 4d). We detected expected cell classes and subclasses in both scRNA-seq GEX libraries (Fig. 4f). Following sequence error correction (Hamming distance ≤1), application of reads per UMI thresholds (mBC >10, oBC >1) and UMI thresholds (mBC >1, oBC >10), we assigned mBCs and oBCs to each cell. Cells containing concordant mBC-oBC pairs were detected across most major cell classes and subclasses (Fig. 4g). Across both Single scQers and Multi scQers, libraries derived from ALM cells consistently exhibited higher numbers of detected oBCs and oBC UMIs as compared to STR cells (P < 2.2 × 10−16 in both Single and Multi-scQers, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Supplementary Fig. 7a–d, “Methods”). In addition, the number of unique oBCs varied systematically by cell class, with the highest levels observed in astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. 7e). Notably, cell class oBC abundance was highly correlated between techniques (Pearson’s r = 0.96, P = 0.00044). Using the number of unique oBCs detected per cell as a proxy for AAV multiplicity of infection, these data demonstrate PHP.eB transduction rates are both cell type- and region-dependent using RO injection in mice, complementing data reported previously23.

We next assessed the concordance between mBCs and their corresponding oBCs and found that only a subset of detected mBCs were concordantly paired with the expected oBC within the same cell (Single scQers: 3450 mBC-oBC concordant pairs/6908 total mBCs, 50%; Multi scQers: 932 mBC-oBC concordant pairs/9452 total mBCs, 10%; Supplementary Fig. 7f, g), despite robust detection of UMIs across oBCs (mean ± standard deviation total UMIs per oBC: Single scQers 572,327 ± 217,182, Multi scQers 2264 ± 3694). The markedly lower mBC-oBC concordance observed in the Multi scQer libraries is likely attributable to the larger barcode space, enabling improved discrimination and filtering of spurious barcode pairings, in combination with AAV packaging-induced chimerism.

Retaining only concordant pairs significantly increased enhancer specificity in the Multi scQer libraries, but not in the Single scQer libraries compared to discordant mBCs alone (Single scQers: P = 0.37; Multi scQers: *P = 0.035; Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Supplementary Fig. 7h). While we observed a strong correlation in enhancer specificities across techniques (Pearson’s r = 0.88, P = 2.8 × 10−7, Supplementary Fig. 7i), we found that even after applying dual barcode-based error correction, apparent enhancer specificities remained significantly lower than those measured by single-agent validation using snRNA-seq and immunohistochemistry (Single scQers ***P = 0.00088, Multi scQers **P = 0.0081, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test) (Fig. 4h, i).

We next asked what additional factors contribute to the loss of apparent enhancer specificity in multiplexed assays. We found that both target cell type abundance (Pearson’s r = −0.67, P = 2.3 × 10−6) and SYFP2 reporter expression levels (Pearson’s r = −0.52, P = 5.2 × 10−4) were negatively correlated with specificity loss in multiplexed screening (Fig. 4j). These relationships indicate that enhancers driving stronger and more broadly detectable expression are more resilient to multiplexing-associated noise. In contrast, mBC UMI counts from mBC-oBC concordant pairs showed little correlation with specificity loss (Pearson’s r = −0.11, P = 0.47), suggesting that spurious mBC detection in multiplexed assays arises through mechanisms largely independent of true enhancer-driven transcription.

While enhancer strength and target cell abundance help explain robustness in multiplexed screens, they do not fully account for the enhancer-independent mBC signal observed. This led us to examine biological mechanisms that could generate apparent off-target expression independent of true enhancer activity.

sec.title: AAV transcriptional crosstalk is a potential source of biological noise
sec.p: Following transduction, AAVs can persist in the nucleus as concatemers37–40. While concatenation promotes long-term transgene expression, this configuration can also induce transcriptional crosstalk between enhancer AAVs, which occurs when an active enhancer from one vector drives expression of another linked vector22. We recapitulated this effect with two individually packaged enhancer AAV vectors that individually express in separate cell populations: Pvalb interneuron-specific AiE0140h_3xC2 (optimized version of AiE0140h) enhancer driving mScarlet and striatal cholinergic-specific AiE0743m_3xC2 enhancer driving SYFP22,6,7. When co-injected together these two vectors exhibit a high degree of overlap in the cortex, as shown previously6 (Genetic Tools Atlas, Supplementary Fig. 8a), but when injected alone, AiE0743m_3xC2-SYFP2 has little activity in cortex, as expected (Genetic Tools Atlas, Supplementary Fig. 8b).

To test whether AAV concatenation contributes to unwanted crosstalk, we used severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID; Prkdcscid/scid) mice, which lack the DNA double-strand break repair enzyme Prkdc and have reduced AAV concatenation22,37. We co-injected the cortical Pvalb interneuron enhancer AiE0140h_3xC2 driving the fluorescent protein mTFP1 and the striatal cholinergic enhancer AiE0743m_3xC2 driving nuclear SYFP2-H2B in both SCID and C57BL/6J mice (Supplementary Fig. 8c). In C57BL/6J mice, we observed extensive co-labeling of SYFP2 and mTFP1, particularly in cortex where double-positive cells comprised 81% of all fluorescent cells, compared to 24% of fluorescent cells in the striatum (Supplementary Fig. 8d, e). In contrast, SCID mice showed a marked reduction in co-labeled cells, with double-positive populations reduced to 16% in cortex and 6% in striatum (Fisher’s Exact Test, CTX ****P < 0.0001, STR *P = 0.0116). Notably, the overall fluorescence of both mTFP1 and SYFP2 were reduced in SCID mice (Supplementary Fig. 8f). These findings confirm that DNA concatenation-dependent enhancer crosstalk can distort enhancer AAV expression patterns, consistent with prior reports22.

We hypothesized this biological phenomenon was also contributing to spurious enhancer mBC detection in our multiplexed libraries. To test this, we co-injected all twenty previously validated, individually packaged enhancer and promoter AAVs encoding nuclear SYFP2-H2B-mBC into either C57BL/6J or SCID mice (Supplementary Fig. 9a). Deep sequencing of the 3′ UTR of the mixed viruses indicated presence of each mBC (Supplementary Fig. 9b and “Methods”). SYFP2-positive whole cells were isolated by FACS from ALM and STR and processed for 10x Genomics v3.1 scRNA-seq alongside targeted mBC library sequencing (Supplementary Fig. 9a, c, d). We observed good overlap of C57BL/6J and SCID cells for the major cell type classes and subclasses (Supplementary Fig. 9e–g), indicating no gross differences in the transcriptional identity of AAV-labeled SCID-derived cells recovered. However, SCID mice exhibited reduced SYFP2 reporter protein levels by FACS (Supplementary Fig. 9c, d), as well as significantly lower mBC abundance in both on-target and off-target cells (on-target: ****P = 1.5 × 10−173, off-target: ****P = 2.4 × 10−102, Dunn’s test followed by Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, Supplementary Fig. 9h), despite robust reads per UMI per cell across libraries (Supplementary Fig. 9i).

When we analyzed the apparent specificities of each enhancer by multiplex testing in SCID mice, we observed a bimodal effect, where 9/20 enhancers (45%) exhibited improved specificities, 5/20 (25%) showed decreased specificities, and 6/20 (30%) displayed similar specificities to that observed in C57BL/6J mice (Supplementary Fig. 9j, k). Of note, the enhancers that showed the greatest apparent specificity gain in SCID mice were striatal enhancers AiE0447h, AiE0450h, AiE0445h_3xC2, and AiE0779m (Supplementary Fig. 9j). In contrast, all three oligodendrocyte-specific enhancers AiE0410m, AiE0401h, and AiE0391h showed the greatest loss of specificity in SCID mice. As double-strand break repair pathways have been shown to differentially affect processing of AAV vectors41, we investigated select repair pathway gene expression in oligodendrocytes but observed no differences between genotypes (Supplementary Fig. 9l). Overall, however, performing a multiplex in SCID mice did not result in a significant improvement in enhancer specificity across the panel (P = 0.757, Wilcoxon rank-sum test). Altogether, these findings indicate that SCID mice can improve apparent enhancer specificity for a subset of enhancers under multiplexed conditions, but this effect is enhancer- and context-dependent and therefore not a general solution to multiplexing-associated noise.

Another strategy we investigated to mitigate enhancer crosstalk is the use of insulator elements, which can block unintended enhancer activation42. To test this, we inserted the insulators hsA2 (5′), hsA4 (3′), or both immediately internal to the ITRs in AAV constructs containing AiE0140h_3xC2 and AiE0743m_3xC2, two enhancers we previously showed to exhibit strong transcriptional crosstalk.

When injected individually, AiE0140h_3xC2 drives expression in Pvalb interneurons in ALM and STR, while AiE0743m_3xC2 remained primarily striatum-specific (Genetic Tools Atlas, Supplementary Fig. 10a, b). As expected, co-injection of enhancer AAVs without insulators resulted in high crosstalk (92% overlap in ALM, 23% in STR; Supplementary Fig. 10c–e). Addition of a 3′ hsA4 insulator alone had little effect (94% in ALM, 21% in STR; ANOVA with Tukey’s adjustment STR: P = 0.94, ALM: P = 0.23). In contrast, inclusion of a 5′ hsA2 insulator markedly reduced crosstalk in STR (6–7%) but not in ALM (93-96%) significantly (STR: ***P = 1.4 × 10−4, ALM: P = 0.56, ANOVA with Tukey’s adjustment, Supplementary Fig. 10f). These findings indicate that insulators can reduce enhancer crosstalk in a context-dependent manner, highlighting both the promise and the remaining limitations of current strategies to mitigate biological noise in multiplexed enhancer AAV screening (Fig. 5).

caption.title: Biological and technical noise strongly influence observed expression in multiplexed enhancer screens.
caption.p: These sources of noise arise at multiple steps, including AAV chimerism during pooled packaging, transcriptional crosstalk by enhancers in vivo, ambient RNA during sample preparation, PCR chimeras during library generation, and other factors specific to the multiplex pool/design.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: With their compact size, cell type specificity, and conservation across species, enhancer elements are becoming increasingly more prevalent as tools for driving specific transgene expression in vivo. However, evaluating enhancer expression remains costly and time-consuming due to the lack of any efficient validation platforms. Using a combination of barcoded enhancer AAV vectors and single-cell RNA sequencing, we aimed to increase screening throughput by adapting a multiplex approach. Instead, we identified multiple caveats including low AAV transcript capture and high technical and biological noise that prevented accurate characterization of all enhancer AAVs. These results demonstrate important caveats to consider when designing an enhancer AAV multiplexed screen.

Low AAV transcript recovery was particularly evident in nuclear preparations, and despite many optimization attempts, we were unable to substantially improve nuclear retention. However, one potential limitation was that all strategies we tested relied on 3′ capture of AAV mRNA transcripts through their poly(A) tails, which may cause a bias towards cytosolic mRNA species. Future studies leveraging 5′-based capture approaches, which do not rely on poly(A)-mediated capture, may improve nuclear AAV transcript recovery and enhance the utility of nuclei-based multiplexing strategies.

Technical noise, derived from spurious ambient RNA, PCR chimeras or sequencing errors, has been extensively documented in droplet-based RNA sequencing34,43–45 and is most likely the cause of low UMI/read counts. In contrast, biological noise is much more difficult to distinguish from true enhancer activity because it reflects bona fide transcription driven by enhancer or AAV interactions, explaining why computational denoising approaches were ineffective in this context. These biological sources of noise obscure multiplexed enhancer expression because they appear as real signal. This also explains why multiplex mBC UMI counts do not correlate well with enhancer-driven protein expression from individual injections.

Beyond enhancer transcriptional crosstalk, we and our co-submitted companion paper (Lalanne et al.) identified a source of biological noise from AAV chimerism occurring during pooled packaging. The observed rate of swapping (~37%) we report aligns with the expected rate for homologous regions of this size, as described in Lalanne et al. This chimerism has likely contributed to high background noise in many published multiplexed AAV screens in the literature record, as well as additional noise in our Multi scQers assay. Because of this, we caution against pooled AAV packaging, which further limits the use of multiplexed enhancer screening. If pooled packaging is required, barcode swap-mitigation strategies include error correction scQer dual barcodes, minimizing vector homology, and packaging with sparse transfection (at the expense of titer). See also the companion manuscript by Lalanne et al. for more discussion of these strategies21.

What was particularly perplexing was that even after minimizing both technical noise through read- and UMI-based filtering, as well as AAV chimerism noise through single packaging, a multiplexed screen in SCID mice should, in principle, have resolved most of the remaining biological noise (transcriptional crosstalk). Yet we observed no overall improvement in enhancer specificity in SCID mice relative to C57BL/6J mice. Why did this approach fail?

One likely explanation is the marked reduction in enhancer-driven expression, both at the protein and mRNA level, which reduces detection sensitivity and has also been shown previously to be linked to AAV concatenation levels41. This effect was region- and cell type-dependent and likely contributes to the observed bimodal distribution of enhancer specificities in SCID multiplexed screening. For example, enhancers targeting oligodendrocytes lost apparent specificity, and enhancers targeting striatal medium spiny neurons gained specificity. Consistent with this interpretation, the Pvalb interneuron enhancer AiE0140h showed reduced enhancer-driven protein expression in the SCID two-plex and correspondingly lost specificity in the SCID multiplex. Although we did not detect overt differences in cell type abundances or DNA repair gene expression in oligodendrocytes, such discrepancies may still reflect differences in expression of the Prkdc loss-of-function allele or differential reliance on Prkdc-mediated DNA repair pathways (homologous versus non-homologous41) across cell types and/or brain regions that are not captured in our datasets46.

A second, more speculative explanation could be an additional, unexplored source of biological noise. The scQer design provided further insight into AAV multiplicity of infection (MOI), revealing higher transduction rates in cortex compared to striatum and across cell types following retro-orbital administration of PHP.eB AAV vectors. Notably, (1) crosstalk was consistently lower in striatal than ALM cells, (2) striatal enhancers exhibited greater specificity gains in SCID mice multiplexing, and (3) 5′ insulators lessened crosstalk in striatum but not ALM. These observations suggest that reducing AAV MOI per cell may help mitigate multiplexing-associated noise. However, heterogeneity in cellular MOI limits uniform application of a low MOI multiplex across cell types/brain regions and having a small barcode space (as in Single scQers, one mBC-oBC per construct) decreases the error-correction potential of oBC-mBC co-detections in high MOI regime since many/most barcodes become present in profiled cells. Additionally, high in vivo MOI could contribute to multiplexing noise through other mechanisms beyond transcriptional crosstalk not yet investigated, such as AAV recombination or cross-hybridization or template switching, which may also be related to the packaging-associated chimerism we observed21. Although speculative, this unexplored source of biological noise could represent a critical missing piece in understanding the limitations of multiplexed enhancer screening.

Our findings strongly suggest that screening diverse enhancers with unknown or heterogeneous specificities in a single pool introduces multiple confounding noise sources. Importantly, many of the high-performing enhancers used here, now deployed for precise cell type targeting in experimental and therapeutic applications, would not have emerged from multiplex screening alone. Thus, in its current form, multiplexed enhancer AAV screening systematically fails to recover many valuable cell type-specific enhancers.

Despite these limitations, enhancer AAV multiplexing may still be useful for narrowly defined screening applications as minimizing noise requires careful consideration of enhancer pool composition, size, and enhancer strength. For example, relatively small pools (e.g., ~twenty-plex) could be used to rank enhancers targeting similar cell types or compare closely related enhancer optimization designs to identify the strongest candidate for a predefined population. In addition, multiplexing followed by single-agent validation may offer cost savings in settings where one-by-one testing is impractical, such as whole-organ primate studies. However, extending this approach to unbiased de novo enhancer discovery will require substantial advances to mitigate both technical and biological sources of noise.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: All experiments were performed in accordance with the Allen Institute Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) (protocols 2002, 2105, 2301, and 2406) and complies with all ethical regulations.

sec.title: Experimental model and subject details
sec.p: All experiments were performed in Mus musculus. Mice were maintained on a C57BL/6J genetic background and were group-housed (maximum five mice per cage) under standard conditions (22–26 °C, 40–60% relative humidity) on a 12-h light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water. Wildtype C57BL/6J mice (Stock No. 000664) and B6.Cg-Prkdcscid/SzJ (SCID mice, Stock No. 001913) were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA). Drd1a-tdTomato line 6 hemizygous mice47 used to quantify striatal MSN enhancer specificities were bred in-house. Mice were injected RO between ages P28-P56 and brains harvested 28–35 days later across all experiments. Sex was not considered in the study design. All enhancers used in this manuscript have been previously published and validated with no reported sex-specific differences in expression patterns. Therefore, sex-specific effects were not expected to impact the study outcomes. All tissue used in this study was derived from male mice, except for tissue used to generate whole cells in Fig. 2, which was derived from a female mouse.

sec.title: Design and cloning of AAV reporter constructs
Cloning for mBC enhancer AAV constructs
sec.p: The 8 bp mBC strategy was derived from Guo et al.48 and all twenty mBCs used in this study were designed to have a Hamming Distance >3. We ordered mBCs as single-stranded forward and reverse complement oligonucleotides (Supplementary Data 2, AIBS_1-40) from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT) with 20 bp overlapping homology regions on either side of the XhoI site in the vector rAAV-hSyn1-SYFP2-10aa-H2B-WPRE3-bGHpA (AiP11839, Addgene 163509). Enhancers and mBCs were uniquely paired using a two-step cloning process.

Enhancers plus minimal promoters were first subcloned from plasmids in-house into AiP11839. Two micrograms of AiP11839 or in-house plasmids containing enhancers plus minimal promoters were digested overnight with 1 µL MluI-HF (NEB R3198L) and 1 µL and AgeI-HF (NEB R3552L) in 10× rCutsmart Buffer (NEB B6004S) diluted in water. The digested backbone (AiP11839) or inserts (enhancers plus promoters) was cleaned by gel extraction on a 1% agarose gel using the Zymoclean Gel DNA Recovery Kit (Zymo Research D4001). Enhancer inserts were then subcloned into the digested AiP11839 using a 2:1 insert:backbone ratio with T4 Quick Ligase (NEB M2200L) for 10 minutes at room temperature. The reactions were then transformed into chemically competent Stbl3 E. coli (ThermoFisher C737303) for 5 min at room temperature and individual colonies were selected from 100 µg/mL carbenicillin plates (Teknova L1010). Plasmids were maxiprepped (Qiagen 12162) and verified using Azenta Sanger sequencing and Plasmidsaurus.

Two micrograms of each enhancer plasmid resulting from the steps above was digested overnight with 1 µL XhoI (NEB R0146L) and 10x rCutsmart Buffer (NEB B6004S) diluted in water. Digested plasmids were cleaned by gel extraction on a 1% agarose gel and the ymoclean Gel DNA Recovery Kit (Zymo Research D4001).

Each lyophilized oligonucleotide stock from IDT was resuspended in water to 100 µM and then combined with its pair and diluted 1:500 in water. Each diluted oligo pair was annealed using by combining 4 µL of diluted oligos with 1 µL of NEB Buffer 4 (NEB B7004S) and 5 µL water and heating the mixture at 100 °C for 5 min and then slowly cooling to room temperature over 30 min using a thermocycler. The annealed oligonucleotides were cloned into the vector in a 10 µL reaction using 2 µL of 5× In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara 639650), 1 µL annealed oligos, and 50 ng of digested plasmid. The reaction was placed at 50 °C for 30 min.

In-Fusion reactions were transformed into chemically competent Stbl3 E. coli (ThermoFisher C737303) for 5 min at room temperature and individual colonies were selected from 100 µg/mL carbenicillin plates. Plasmids were maxiprepped (Qiagen 12162) and verified using Azenta Sanger sequencing. This resulted in 20 mBC enhancer AAV plasmids (Supplementary Data 3).

sec.title: Cloning for single scQers
sec.p: To generate dual barcoded enhancer AAV vectors, oBC systems were ordered as IDT Gblocks containing 5′ broccoli, unique 15 bp oBC, 10× capture sequence 1 (CS1), 3′ broccoli, 3′ tornado ribozyme, U6 terminator, and 20 bp parent vector overhangs (Supplementary Data 3). Then, all 20 mBC enhancer AAV vectors from above were digested overnight at 37 °C with MluI-HF or MluI-HF (for enhancers) and XbaI (for promoters hSyn1 and CMV), extracted from a 1% agarose gel, and isolated using a gel extraction kit (Zymo Research D4001). IDT oBC Gblocks were resuspended to 25 ng/µL in TE buffer and ligated into digested parent vector using In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara 639650), similar to mBC cloning strategy above. In-Fusion reactions were transformed into chemically competent Stbl3 E. coli (ThermoFisher C737303) and individual colonies were selected from 100 µg/mL carbenicillin plates. Plasmids were maxiprepped (Qiagen 12162) and verified for correct oBC sequence as well as correct oBC-enhancer-mBC pairing using Plasmidsaurus whole plasmid sequencing.

sec.title: Cloning for multi scQers
sec.p: The Multi scQers library was made through a collaboration with the Shendure lab at the University of Washington and full details on the library and oBC-enhancer-mBC dictionary construction can be found in the co-submitted manuscript Lalanne et al.21 under the “Methods” subsections “Cloning scQer-AAV libraries with 20 validated enhancer-promoter pairs” and “Creation of oBC-enhancer-mBC association dictionary for scQer constructs”. As a high-level overview, the library construction is broken down into three parts. First, a cloning dock plasmid was constructed using a XhoI/PacI digested AiP11839 and then Gibson assembly was used to insert hU6 promoter + homology arms (PCR amplified from an in-house plasmid) and Gblock containing the start of the Tornado ribozyme, double SapI sites, and homology arms. The resulting plasmid was verified by whole plasmid sequencing (Plasmidsaurus). Second, the scQer library was constructed through an intermediate complex pool linking oBCs, enhancers, promoters, and mBCs. oBC, mBC, and enhancer-promoter fragments were generated separately and assembled in individual reactions by overlap extension PCR, followed by equimolar pooling. The complex assembled oBC-enhancer-promoter-mBC fragments were cloned into the above plasmid by Gibson assembly and electroporated into E. coli, with library complexity controlled by bottlenecking. Library quality was assessed by colony PCR and Sanger sequencing, and the resulting intermediate library was used to generate a barcode-enhancer dictionary for downstream analyses. Lastly, the intermediate construct was digested with the homing endonuclease I-SceI to open the region between the promoter and mBC, followed by agarose size selection. A reporter cassette (SYFP2-H2B-WPRE3), PCR-amplified from AiP11839, was inserted by Gibson assembly, and correct constructs were confirmed by colony PCR and Sanger sequencing after bacterial transformation. The validated library was expanded and purified by midiprep for pooled AAV packaging.

To generate the oBC-enhancer-mBC dictionary, the intermediate plasmid library lacking the reporter insert was PCR-amplified to append P5 and P7 Illumina adapters and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 using custom primers, with read architectures capturing the mBC (Read 1), sample index (Index 1), oBC (Index 2), and enhancer sequence (Read 2). Following enhancer alignment using Bowtie249 and custom data processing for oBC and mBC, the final dictionary was confirmed to contain 3614 unique oBC-enhancer-mBC triplets. This dictionary was used as the ground-truth for determining enhancer specificities.

AAV packaging chimerism was assessed in this library at a rate of 9% and 45% depending on the length of the homology regions (220 bp vs 1450 bp). Details describing the sequencing and results can be found in the co-submitted manuscript Lalanne et al.21 under “Methods” subsection “Data analysis of ONT libraries for scQer constructs” and in accompanying Fig. S9 and results section. Please contact jean-benoit.lalanne@umontreal.ca and shendure@uw.edu for reagent sharing requests or for more information.

sec.title: Cloning for improving AAV transcript detection in the nucleus
sec.p: For cloning different vector designs with or without the WPRE3, AiP11839 (rAAV-hSyn1-SYFP2-10aa-H2B-WPRE3-bGHpA, Addgene 163509) was used as the parent vector. All inserts were synthesized as Gblocks (IDT) with 20 bp homology arms (Supplementary Data 2, AIBS_61-66). AiP11839 was first digested overnight at 37 °C using BmtI/PmlI, run on a 1% agarose gel and gel extracted using a gel extraction kit (Zymo Research). Gblocks were cloned using In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara 639650) at 50 °C for 30 min. In-Fusion reactions were transformed into chemically competent Stbl3 E. coli (ThermoFisher C737303) similar to mBC strategy above and individual colonies were selected from 100 µg/mL carbenicillin plates. Plasmids were maxiprepped (Qiagen 12162) and verified using Azenta Sanger sequencing. The 8 bp barcode was then synthesized as a duplexed oligo with 20 bp overlapping homology arms (Supplementary Data 2, AIBS_67-70) and inserted into the resulting plasmid by digesting with EcoRV, purifying by gel extraction (Zymo Research) and using the In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara 639650) at 50 °C for 30 min. In-Fusion reactions were transformed into chemically competent Stbl3 E. coli (ThermoFisher C737303) and individual colonies were selected from 100 µg/mL carbenicillin plates. Plasmids were maxiprepped (Qiagen 12162) and verified using Azenta Sanger sequencing.

For generation of AiP13257, KASH was synthesized as a Gblock (IDT) with 20 bp homology arms (Supplementary Data 2, AIBS_71). AiP12805 (rAAV-hSyn1-SYFP2-10aa-H2B-WPRE3-barcode-bGHpA) was digested overnight at 37 °C using AgeI-HF/EcoRV-HF, purified using the gel extraction kit (Zymo Research), and inserted using In-Fusion kit, as described above.

For cloning of U7 systems and BORG motifs, AiP13968 (rAAV-DLX2.0-minBG-SYFP2-10aa-H2B-WPRE3-barcode-bGHpA) was used as the parent vector. Twelve different designs were chosen and synthesized as either ultramers (IDT) or Gblocks (IDT) with 20 bp homology arms (smOPT-stem loop-3’ box; smOPT-stem loop; 3xsmOPT; 3xsmOPT-stem loop; 1xBORG; 3xBORG, Supplementary Data 2 AIBS_72-83). AiP13968 was digested overnight at 37 °C using different restriction enzymes depending on the insert design and location (5′ or 3′ of the SYFP2-H2B). NheI-HF/AgeI-HF for synthesizing AiP14787 and AIP14793; EcoRI-HF/EcoRV-HF for synthesizing AiP14788, AiP14794, and AiP14798; SacI-HF/AgeI-HF for synthesizing AiP14789, AiP14791, AiP14795, and AiP14797; EcoRI-HF/XhoI for synthesizing AiP14790, AiP14792, and AiP14796. The resulting digested AiP13968 was extracted using a 1% agarose gel and purified using a gel extraction kit (Zymo Research). All designs were inserted using In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara 639650) at 50 °C for 30 min. In-Fusion reactions were transformed into chemically competent Stbl3 E. coli (ThermoFisher C737303) and individual colonies were selected from 100 µg/mL carbenicillin plates. Plasmids were maxiprepped (Qiagen 12162) and verified using Azenta Sanger sequencing.

sec.title: Cloning for insertion of insulators
sec.p: Insulator elements hsA2 and hsA4 were ordered with 20 bp overlapping regions to AiP13038 and AiP13895 (Addgene 191720) as Gblocks (Supplementary Data 2, AIBS_84-87). Plasmids were digested overnight at 37 °C with MluI-HF in Cutsmart. The resulting digested plasmids were extracted using a 1% agarose gel and purified using a gel extraction kit (Zymo Research). hsA2 designs were inserted using In-Fusion HD Cloning Kit (Takara 639650) at 50 °C for 30 min. In-Fusion reactions were transformed into chemically competent Stbl3 E. coli (ThermoFisher C737303) and individual colonies were selected from 100 µg/mL carbenicillin plates. Plasmids were maxiprepped (Qiagen 12162) and verified using Azenta Sanger sequencing. HsA4 designed were then cloned in using the resulting plasmids digested with PmlI in Cutsmart overnight at 37 °C and the same strategy as stated for cloning in hsA2.
Sequences and metadata for all vectors used in this study can be found in Supplementary Data 3. All plasmid sequences are also deposited to GenBank under accession codes PZ036121-PZ036182.

sec.title: AAV production
sec.p: All plasmids used in this study were packaged into the AAV capsid PHP.eB23 using a small-scale crude prep packaging method as described previously6,12. HEK293T cells (ATCC CRL-11268) were seeded at 2E7 cells per 15-cm dish to achieve ∼70%–80% confluency before transfection. Cells were maintained in DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific Cat#1995-065) with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS; VWR Cat#89510-184) and 1% Antibiotic-Antimycotic solution (Sigma Cat#A5955). Small-scale crude AAV preps were generated by triple transfecting 15 µg ITR plasmid, 15 µg AAV PHP.eB capsid plasmid, and 30 µg pHelper (Cell Biolabs) in 1.35 ml of OptiMem (Thermo Fisher Scientific Cat#51985-034), which was then supplemented with 150 µl of 1 mg/mL Polyethylenimine (PEI; Polysciences Cat#23966), incubated for 10 minutes and then added to a single 15 cm plate of fully confluent cells. For pooled packaging, plasmids were combined at equal ratios for a total of 15 µg. At 1 day post-transfection medium was replaced with low serum (1% FBS), and after 3 days the cells and supernatant were collected, freeze-thawed 3× to release AAV particles, treated with benzonase nuclease (Millipore Sigma E8263-25KU) for 30 min to degrade free DNA, then clarified (3000 × g × 10 min) and concentrated to approximately 150 µL by using an Amicon Ultra-15 centrifugal filter unit (Sigma Cat # UFC910024) at 5000 × g for 30–60 min. Viral prep titers were assessed using digital droplet PCR (BioRad QX200 system) using primers against AAV2 ITRs and typically resulted in around 100 µL of 1-5E13 vg/mL per virus.

sec.title: Short read sequencing of mBC amplicons from enhancer AAV multiplex pools
sec.p: To confirm representation of all 6 mBCs in individual or pooled six-plexes and 20 mBCs in twenty-plex, viruses were diluted 1:1000 in water, denatured at 100 °C for 5 min, and PCR amplified using KAPA HiFi Mastermix (Roche 7958935001) with forward primer 5′ AACTCATCGCCGCCTGCCTTG 3′ and reverse primer 5′ ACAGTGGGAGTGGCACCTTC 3′ for 30 cycles. Following amplification, reactions were purified using 0.6× and 0.9× SPRI beads (Beckman Coulter B23317), resuspended in 25 µL Buffer EB, and sequenced using Azenta Amplicon-EZ sequencing service. Sequencing fastq reads were imported into R using the R package ShortRead50 and mBCs were identified using both Read 1 and Read 2 using string_detect from R package stringr. All six barcodes were confirmed to be present in both types of six-plex pools and all twenty barcodes were confirmed in the twenty-plex pools (Supplementary Data 4).

sec.title: Oxford Nanopore technology (ONT) sequencing and analysis
sec.p: To assess recombination during pooled AAV packaging, six AAV preparations (three individually packaged and three pooled) were sequenced using Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing (Plasmidsaurus AAV Genome Sequencing service35). Raw reads were aligned to the six AAV reference genomes using minimap251 (-ax map-ont). SAM files were converted to BAM format with samtools52 and imported into R using Rsamtools53. Reads shorter than 2100 bp (minimum ITR-to-ITR enhancer genome length) or longer than 3000 bp (to restrict analysis to single-genome molecules) were excluded. mBCs were identified using str_detect (R package stringr54). The percentage of valid enhancer-mBC pairs was calculated as the number of mapped reads containing a valid enhancer-mBC pair divided by the number of mapped reads containing an mBC, multiplied by 100. The total reads remaining at each step is outlined in Supplementary Data 5.

sec.title: Retro-orbital mouse injections
sec.p: PHP.eB-packaged AAVs were first diluted either individually (5E11 vg) or in a pool (6E11-1E12 total vg) for the multiplex experiments in 100 μL of sterile 1× PBS. Adult P28-P56 male mice were injected with the diluted AAVs into the retro-orbital sinus after isoflurane anesthesia. Tissue was harvested 4–5 weeks post-injection for all experiments.

sec.title: Mouse regional brain dissections
sec.p: Mice were anesthetized with Avertin and perfused transcardially with either ice-cold Cutting Buffer containing 110 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 7.5 mM MgCl2, 25 mM glucose, and 75 mM sucrose for cell isolations or 1xPBS for nuclear isolations. Following perfusions, brains were extracted and placed in a petri dish containing Cutting Buffer (cells) or 1× PBS (nuclei) to generate 2 mm coronal slices using a stainless-steel brain matrix (Stoelting 51386). Slices containing ALM or STR were transferred to a second petri dish with Dissociation Buffer containing 82 mM Na2SO4, 30 mM K2SO4, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM Glucose, and 5 mM MgCl2 (cells) or 1× PBS (nuclei). ALM and STR were isolated from the coronal sections using a disposable safety scalpel (VWR 21909-670). Tissue pieces were then processed immediately for cell isolations or placed in 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes, flash frozen in a dry ice-ethanol bath and stored at −80 °C for nuclei isolations.

sec.title: Single cell suspensions
sec.p: Cell suspensions were prepared as previously described55. After dissection, ALM, or STR were placed separately in 10 mL conical tubes with 5 mL of room temperature Enzyme Buffer containing 3 mg/mL Protease XXIII (Sigma-Aldrich P5380) and 10 units/mL of Papain (Worthington LK003150) dissolved in Dissociation Buffer. Submerged slides were immediately transferred to a 34 °C water bath for 1 h (STR) or 2 h (ALM). Following digestion, tissue was placed directly on ice and the supernatant was carefully removed and replaced with 10 mL Stop Solution containing 1 mg/mL Trypsin Inhibitor (Sigma-Aldrich T6522), 2 mg/mL BSA (Sigma-Aldrich A2153), and 1 mg/mL Ovomucoid Protease Inhibitor (Worthington LK003150) dissolved in Dissociation Buffer. Tissue chunks were triturated using four fire-polished glass Pasteur pipets with successively smaller bore holes while avoiding bubbles until a homogenous solution was obtained. Triturated tissue was centrifuged at 300 × g for 10 min at 4 °C, supernatant decanted, pellet resuspended in 5 mL of Stop Solution and then centrifuged again at 300 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Following centrifugation, the supernatant was decanted once more and the cell pellet was resuspended in 500 µL= to 1 mL of Dissociation Buffer with 0.1% BSA, 1:500 DAPI (ThermoFisher 62248), and 1:500 Vibrant DyeCycle Ruby Stain (ThermoFisher V10309). The resulting single-cell suspensions were filtered using a pre-wet 70 µm filter (Miltenyi Biotec 130-098-462) and incubated in the dark at 4 °C for 30 min prior to flow cytometry.

sec.title: Single-nucleus suspensions
sec.p: Single-nucleus isolations were prepped as described previously25. In summary, 250 mL of Nuclei Isolation Media (pH = 8) containing 250 mM sucrose, 10 mM Tris Buffer (pH = 8), 25 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl2 was prepared ahead of time and placed at 4 °C for up to 2 weeks. Next, 2 mL glass dounces with their accompanying A and B pestles (Sigma-Aldrich D8938) were placed in RNase Away solution (VWR 53225-514) overnight at room temperature. The following day, the dounces were rinsed thoroughly with MilliQ water and air dried. Dounces were placed on ice and filled with 1.5 mL of Homogenization Buffer containing 0.1 mM DTT (Promega P1171), 1x Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Promega G6521), 0.2 U/µL RNasin Plus RNase Inhibitor (Promega N2615), 0.1% Triton X-100 dissolved in 0.22 μm filtered Nuclei Isolation Media. Previously frozen ALM or STR tissue punches were retrieved from −80 °C and transferred to the Homogenization Buffer-filled dounces. Tissue was homogenized 15–20× with Pestle A, followed by 10-15x with Pestle B and then filtered through a 70 µm filter (Miltenyi Biotec 130-098-462) on top of a 15 mL conical tube. An additional 3 mL of Homogenization Buffer was added and then the tissue was centrifuged at 900 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Following centrifugation, the supernatant was discarded, and the nuclei pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of Blocking Buffer containing 1x PBS (pH = 7.4), 1% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich A9576), 0.2 U/µL RNasin Plus RNase Inhibitor, and transferred to a 1.5 mL Eppendorf tube. DAPI (0.1 µg/mL) and 1:500 mouse monoclonal anti NeuN conjugated to PE (Sigma-Aldrich FCMAB317PE) was added to the tube and incubated at 4 °C for 30 min in the dark, then centrifuged at 400 × g for 5 min at 4 °C. Supernatant was decanted, and nuclei pellet was resuspended in 500 μL of Blocking Buffer and filtered through the cap of a 5 mL FACS tube (Fisher Scientific 08-771-23) on ice prior to flow cytometry.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: Cell and nuclei suspensions were sorted for SYFP2 expression using a 130 µm nozzle on a BD FACSAria III at a flow rate of <2000 cells/nuclei per second on purity mode. Live cells were selected for by a DAPI-negative, Ruby-positive gate and intact nuclei by a DAPI-positive gate. A goal of 50-100,000 SYFP2-positive and SYFP2-negative cells and nuclei were collected in chilled 5 mL FACS tubes containing 300 μL Dissociation Buffer with 0.1% BSA (cells) or Blocking Buffer (nuclei). Following FACS, 30% Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA) was added to the sorted nuclei for a final concentration of 2%, centrifuged at 500xg for 5 minutes at 4 °C, and all but ~50 μL of supernatant above the pellet was decanted. The nuclei were resuspended in Freezing Media containing 1xPBS, 1% BSA, 10% DMSO (Millipore-Sigma 276855), and 0.2 U/µL of RNasin Plus RNase Inhibitor at a 1:1 ratio and frozen at −80 °C until loading on the 10x Genomics v3.1 chip (1000268, 10× Genomics) later. The sorted cells were centrifuged at 300 × g for 10 min at 4 °C, supernatant decanted, and the pellet resuspended in 80-100 μL of Dissociation Buffer with 0.1% BSA on ice. Cell concentrations were estimated using a disposable hemocytometer (Thomas Scientific 1190G82) on a Nikon Ti-Eclipse microscope and were immediately loaded on the 10x v3.1 or v4 chip for insertion into the 10x Genomics Chromium controller.

sec.title: SMART-Seq v4 single-nucleus library prep and RNA sequencing
sec.p: Single nucleus suspensions from mice with individual enhancer AAV RO injections were prepared for flow cytometry as described above under “Single nucleus suspensions”. 800 single nuclei (40 nuclei per ALM/STR per enhancer) were sorted into 8-well strips containing SMART-Seq lysis buffer with RNase inhibitor (0.17 U/μL; Takara Cat# ST0764) on ice and were immediately frozen at −80 °C. SMART-Seq reagents (Takara Cat# 634894). were used for reverse transcription and cDNA amplification following the manufacturer’s protocol. Samples were tagmented and indexed using a NexteraXT DNA Library Preparation kit (Illumina Cat#FC-131-1096) with NexteraXT Index Kit V2 Set A (Illumina Cat#FC-131-2001) according to manufacturer’s instructions except for decreases in volumes of all reagents, including cDNA, to 0.4 x recommended volume. Full documentation for the snRNA-seq procedure is available in the ‘Documentation’ section of the Allen Institute data portal at http://celltypes.brain-map.org/. All 800 nuclei were sequenced except 1 nucleus that did not have a cDNA product. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 as 50 bp paired end reads. Reads were aligned to GRCm38 (genecode v23) using STAR v2.7.1 with the parameter “twopassMode,” and exonic read counts were quantified using the GenomicRanges package for R as described in Tasic et al.56. To determine the corresponding cell type for each snRNA-seq dataset, we utilized MapMyCells hierarchical mapping (RRID: SCR_024672) from the Allen Institute http://celltypes.brain-map.org/ according to the posted instructions against the 10× Whole mouse brain taxonomy (CCN20230722). We applied quality control steps to exclude cells from the dataset if they had less than 500 genes detected (18 nuclei; 2%) and if they clearly did not map to cell subclasses corresponding to the dissected brain regions (37 nuclei; 5%). The remaining 744 high-quality nuclei (93%) were used to determine enhancer AAV labeling specificities. Enhancer specificities were calculated as number of SYFP2+ nuclei on-target divided by the total number of nuclei multiplied by 100 to obtain a percentage.

sec.title: 10x Genomics, custom AAV mBC/oBC library generation, and sequencing
sec.p: Previously sorted nuclei were removed from the −80 °C and allowed to thaw on ice. One hundred microliters of Nuclei Wash and Resuspension Buffer containing 1% BSA, 0.2U/µL Rnasin Plus RNase Inhibitor in 1x PBS was added to the nuclei and then centrifuged at 400 × g for 5 min at 4 °C. Following centrifugation, the supernatant was removed, and the nuclei pellet was resuspended in ~50 µL of Nuclei Wash and Resuspension Buffer. Nuclei concentrations were estimated using a disposable hemocytometer and concentration was adjusted to 1000 nuclei/μL using Nuclei Wash and Resuspension Buffer. Approximately ~16,000 cells or nuclei were loaded on the 10× Genomics v3.1 chip (PN-1000268, 10× Genomics) or v4 chip (PN-1000686, 10× Genomics).

For GEX library generation from samples just containing mBC enhancer AAVs, the manufacturer’s instructions for cell capture, barcoding, reverse transcription, cDNA amplification and library construction were followed. Libraries were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 or NovaSeq X with a target read depth of 125,000 reads per cell/nuclei.

For GEX library generation from Single scQers, the protocol from the manufacturer for 10x Genomics v4 was followed exactly until step 2.2a (cDNA amplification from v4 manual CG000731 Rev B, 10× Genomics). At this step we made two modifications. (1) The cDNA primers were replaced with Feature cDNA Primers 1 (PN-2000096) which is critical to retain oBC transcripts. (2) We also spiked-in primers specific to the mBC (5′ GTGAACCGCATCGAGCTGAA 3′) and oBC (5′ AACCATGCCGAGTGCGG 3′) to a final concentration of 0.5 µM. Following cDNA amplification, we followed the clean-up procedures for 10× v3.1 feature barcoding (v3.1 manual CG000205 Rev D, 10× Genomics, with gene expression and mBC components in the pellet fraction 2.3Ax, and oBC in the supernatant fraction 2.3Bxiv). After step 2.3, gene expression libraries are completed and sequenced following the v4 user manual.

sec.title: mBC library generation
sec.p: To generate custom libraries for the AAV mBC transcripts, 10 ng of the amplified cDNA from each sample was first amplified in a 100 μL reaction containing 50 µL KAPA Hifi Mastermix (Roche 7958935001), 0.5 µL 100 µM forward WPRE3 primer 5′ AACTCATCGCCGCCTGCCTTG 3′ and 0.5 µL 100 µM reverse Read 1 primer 5′ CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT 3′ and amplified using a thermocycler with the following conditions: 98 °C for 5 min initial denaturation, then 8 cycles of 95 °C for 15 s, 60 °C for 30 seconds, 72 °C for 20 s, and lastly 72 °C for 30 s. The reaction was purified using 0.7X and 0.9X SPRI beads (Beckman Coulter B23318) and then resuspended in 40 µL Buffer EB (Qiagen 19086). Sequencing adapters and indexed were added using 20 µL of product from the first PCR along with 0.5 µL of 100 µM nested forward primer 5′ AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACNNNNNNNNNNACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT 3′, 0.5 µL of 100 µM reverse primer 5′ CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATNNNNNNNNNNGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTCTTCCGATCTACTGACAATTCCGTGGCTCG 3′, and 50 µL KAPA HiFi MasterMix. Reaction was amplified using 12 cycles (same thermocycler protocol as above), purified using 0.7X and 0.9X SPRI beads, resuspended in 25 µL Buffer EB, and checked for purity and concentration using the High Sensitivity Kit (Agilent 067-4626) on a Bioanalyzer. The full Bioanalyzer virtual gels from Fig. 2g is provided in the Source Data file.

sec.title: oBC library generation (for Single scQers)
sec.p: oBC libraries were generated as described previously36 with several modifications. A 100 μL reaction containing 6 µL of supernatant fraction from step 2.3Bxiv, 50 µL KAPA Hifi Mastermix (Roche 7958935001), 0.5 µL 100 µM forward Index primer 5′ AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACNNNNNNNNNNACACTCGTCGGCAGCGTCAGATGTGTATAAGAGACAG 3′ and 0.5 µL 100uM reverse Index primer 5′ caagcagaagacggcatacgagatNNNNNNNNNNGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTCTTCCGATCTatgccgagtgcggccgcgaga 3′ were combined and placed in a thermocycler and amplified with the following conditions: 98 °C for 5 minutes initial denaturation, then 9 cycles of 95 °C for 20 s, 60 °C for 20 s, 72 °C for 20 s, and final extension at 72 °C for 30 s. The reaction was purified using 0.6X and 1.2X SPRI beads and resuspended in 20 µL buffer EB. To avoid loop-the-loop products, the lowest band (<300 bp) was removed by an additional SPRI cleanup of 0.75X followed by 1X. The final product was confirmed using the High Sensitivity Kit (Agilent 067-4626) on a Bioanalyzer.

mBC libraries were either sequenced alone or pooled with oBC and sequenced using the following structure: Read 1: 28 cycles (cell barcode, UMI); Index 1: 10 cycles; Index 2: 10 cycles Read 2: 91 cycles.

sec.title: mBC and oBC library generation (for Multi scQers)
sec.p: Preparation of scQer libraries was generated by the Shendure lab and followed the previously described protocol36 with the following minor modifications to be adapted to the new constructs. During the initial cDNA amplification (Step 2.2a in 10x v3.1 user manual CG000205 Rev D, 10× Genomics), specific primers were added to a final concentration of 0.5 µM to selectively enrich for reporter barcodes (oBC: 5′ aaccatgccgagtgcgg 3′, mBC: 5′ CGTGTCCGAGGGTACTAAGG 3′). Gene expression and oBC libraries were then prepared as before. mBC libraries were prepared from 1 µL of 1/10× dilution (approximately 5 ng) of the “pellet” fraction of the purified cDNA amplification by PCR with primers 5′ AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT 3′ and 5′ atccatggccctcaggcatactgttccaactccaCCGAGGGTACTAAGGCCATC 3’ (tracking reaction by qPCR and stopping at inflection point, about 15 to 22 cycles depending on samples). A two-sided Ampure beads clean up (0.5x and 0.7x) was performed and samples eluted in 12 µL. This was finally followed by an indexing PCR with 5′ AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACAC 3′ and 5′ CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATNNNNNNNNNNATCCATGGCCCTCAGGCATAC 3′ with 1 µL of PCR2 purified products in 10 µL reactions for 7 cycles Gene expression, oBC, and mBC libraries were then sequenced on the same NextSeq 2000 flowcell with the following custom read architecture and sequencing primers. Gene expression: read1: oJBL755 (Truseq read1) 28 cycles cell barcode and UMI, index1: oJBL756 (Truseq index1) 10 cycles index P7, index2: oJBL758 (Truseq index2) 10 cycles index P5, read2: oJBL687 (Truseq read2) 90 cycles. oBC: read1 oJBL759 (Nextera R1) 28 cycles cell barcode and UMI, index1: oJBL432 10 cycles index P7, index2: oJBL762 (Nextera idx2) 10 cycles index P5, read2: oJBL433 90 cycles oBC. mBC: read1: oJBL755 (Truseq read 1) 28 cycles cell barcode and UMI, index1: oJBL534 10 cycles sample index P5, index2: oJBL758 (Truseq index 2) 10 cycles P5 index, read2: oJBL920 90 cycles mBC.

sec.title: Sequencing data processing and QC filtering
GEX libraries
sec.p: A custom reference was created using the 10× Genomics Cellranger mkref to add the AAV vector sequence SYFP2-H2B-WPRE3-[mBC]-bGHpA to the mouse reference transcriptome (M21, GRCm38.p6). Sequencing fastq read files were aligned to the custom reference using the 10x Genomics Cell Ranger pipeline (version 6.1.2 for 10x v3.1) with default parameters except for scQers which was aligned to the default mouse reference transcriptome (M21, GRCm38.p6) using the 10x Genomics Cell Ranger pipeline (Multi scQers: version 6.1.2 for 10x v3.1, Single scQers: version 8.0.1 for 10x v4). High-quality cells and nuclei were selected for using stringent QC filtering27,56 using the following filters in R: mitochondrial gene percentage (<5% for nuclei, <20% for cells), total genes detected (>1000 for nuclei, >2000 for cells) and a doublet score of >0.3 using DoubletFinder57. Following QC filtering, cell and nuclei gene x cell count matrices were normalized using logCPM and mapped using map_by_cor (both part of R package scrattch.hicat RRID:SCR_018099) or converted into h5ad files and mapped using MapMyCells (RRID:SCR_024672) onto the CCN20230722 whole mouse brain taxonomy27. Cells or nuclei were discarded if they did not map to cell types in the corresponding region (either ALM or STR) and if they did not map with at least 80% confidence to the reference taxonomy.

sec.title: AAV genome aligned reads from GEX libraries
sec.p: AAV reads were processed using custom scripts with the assistance of OpenAI’s ChatGPT (GPT-4/5) for code development. Aligned reads are extracted from the Cellranger output file possorted_genome_bam.bam using samtools view followed by a custom python script that summarizes read counts per cell barcode-UMI (any AAV aligned reads) or per cell barcode-mBC-UMI (mBC-containing reads) combination. Scripts are deposited at Zenodo58 [10.5281/zenodo.18753067].

sec.title: mBCs and oBCs from barcode libraries
sec.p: AAV mBC and oBC libraries were processed using custom scripts with the assistance of OpenAI’s ChatGPT (GPT-4/5) for code development, including data processing and visualization scripts. Briefly, this is separated into the following steps: (1) extract cell barcodes and UMIs from read 1 based on position in read (position 1 for cell barcode and position 17 for UMI); (2) extract mBC or oBC from read 2 based on position in read (position 23 for mBC and position 40 for oBC); (3) reads are sorted and joined; (4) reads are filtered based on provided cell and AAV barcode sequences (allowing ≤1 Hamming distance error correction); (5) UMIs and reads are summarized per enhancer mBC/oBC per cell.

mBC and oBC read counts were combined with the mapped GEX metadata to determine enhancer specificities. Various cut-offs for reads-per-UMI and UMI counts were used to try to determine enhancer specificities as shown in the relevant figures and explained in the Results text. Scripts are deposited at Zenodo [10.5281/zenodo.18753067].

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Mice injected with enhancer AAVs were anesthetized with Avertin and perfused transcardially with ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). All enhancer AAVs were injected into C57BL/6J mice except for D1 MSN enhancer AiE0779m and D2 MSN enhancers AiE0445h_3xC2 and AiE0452h which were injected in Drd1a-tdTomato line 6 hemizygous mice. The brain was extracted and placed in 4% PFA overnight, then transferred to 30% sucrose in PBS for 2–3 days. Brains were cut in half and mounted on a thin block of OCT cryo-compound (Tissue-Tek # 4583) on a frozen sliding microtome for generation of 30 µm sagittal sections. Sections were stored in PBS with 0.02% sodium azide at 4 °C. For IHC, stored slices were washed 3× in PBS and then placed in blocking buffer containing 5% normal goat serum, 0.1% TritonX-100 in PBS, and primary antibody(ies) at 4 °C overnight. All primary antibodies were diluted to a 1:1000 concentration except for mouse SATB1 + SATB2 which was used at 1:250. The following day, sections were washed 3x in wash buffer containing 0.1% TritonX-100 in PBS and then placed in blocking buffer with appropriate secondary antibodies diluted 1:1000 for 2 h at room temperature. Secondary antibodies included Alexa Fluor 488 Goat anti Chicken (ThermoFisher A11039), Alexa Fluor 555 Goat anti Rabbit (ThermoFisher A32732), Alexa Fluor 555 Goat anti Mouse IgG1 (ThermoFisher A21127), and Alexa Fluor 555 Goat anti Mouse IgG2b (ThermoFisher A21147). Sections were washed 3x in wash buffer and then mounted onto microscope slides using Prolong Gold and imaged at 10x on a Nikon Ti-Eclipse or Nikon Ti-Eclipse 2 epifluorescent microscope.

Specificity of enhancer activity for all enhancers (except D2 MSN enhancers) for the target cell subclass or type was quantified as reporter and marker antibody double positive neuron count divided by total reporter antibody positive neuron count and multiplied by 100 to obtain a percentage.

Specificity for D2 MSN enhancers injected into Drd1a-tdTomato mice was determined by quantifying non-overlapping populations (1 - reporter and marker antibody double positive neuron count divided by total reporter Ab positive neuron count and multiplied by 100 to obtain a percentage). An important caveat to this strategy is it would include any labeling of striatal interneuron populations as on-target. However, both our mapping (Fig. 4) and published validations (Hunker et al.6) suggest interneuron labeling is minimal for these enhancers.

Enhancer on-target specificities were determined using the following antibodies: Chicken polyclonal anti GFP (1:1000, Aves GFP-1010, lot GFP3717982); Rabbit polyclonal anti NeuN (1:1000, Millipore ABN78, lot 3916677); Mouse monoclonal anti S-100 clone SHB1 (β subunit) (1:1000, Sigma S2532, lot 131551); Mouse monoclonal anti APC [CC-1] clone CC-1 (1:1000, Abcam ab16794, lot GR3319170-5); Rabbit polyclonal anti GABA (1:1000, Sigma A2052, lot 462544); Mouse anti SATB1 + SATB2 antibody clone SATBA4B10 (1:250, Abcam ab51502, lot GR3411543-1); Rabbit polyclonal anti Parvalbumin (1:1000, Swant PV27a, lot 2014); Mouse monoclonal anti DARPP-32 Clone 15/DARPP-32 (1:1000, BD Biosciences 611520, lot 2018601); Rabbit polyclonal anti RFP (1:1000, Rockland 600-401-379, lot 48710); Rabbit polyclonal anti somatostatin-28 (1:1000, Peninsula Labs T-4547, lot A18213); Mouse monoclonal anti ChAT clone CL3169 (1:1000, Atlas AMAb91129, lot MAB-03887); Rat anti mTFP (1:1000, CancerTools 155264, lot 2022FB).

sec.title: Statistics and reproducibility
sec.p: No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Cells/nuclei from 10x libraries were excluded from the analyses based on the quality control metrics described in the “Methods” section above (based on number of genes detected, doublet score, and percent of mitochondrial genes). We also used different read/UMI filtering thresholds to remove technical noise on the mBC and oBC libraries as shown in the figures and described in the “Results” section. The experiments were not randomized. The Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment, except for quantification of the effect of Insulator elements described in Supplementary Fig. 10.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: SMART-Seq v4 (Takara) and 10x Genomics 3′ GEX v3.1 and v4 raw and processed sequencing data along with appropriate mBC and oBC PCR library sequencing data generated in this paper have been deposited in GEO under accession code GSE312364. All plasmid sequences used for generating the data in this study have been deposited to Genbank under unique accession codes (one code per plasmid) PZ036121-PZ036182 and can also be found in Supplementary Data 3. Allen Institute for Brain Science whole mouse brain taxonomy CCN2023722 is publicly available for mapping scRNA-seq datasets (RRID:SCR_024672) [https://brain-map.org/bkp/analyze/mapmycells#taxonomies]. Additional mouse brain images for each enhancer AAV is available on the Allen Institute for Brain Science Genetic Tools Atlas (RRID:SCR_025643) [https://brain-map.org/bkp/experiment/genetic-tools/genetic-tools-atlas]. Source data are provided with this paper.
Scripts for processing mBC and oBC UMI counts from GEX libraries, oBC amplicon libraries, and mBC amplicon libraries were deposited to Zenodo58 [10.5281/zenodo.18753067].
